# DashBio {.divider}

[Interactive Plotly widgets for genomics]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 33 -->
## Install & Import {.smaller}

[DashBio · setup]{.eyebrow}

### Plotly figure-generators built for bioinformatics — no Dash server needed

`dash-bio` is Plotly's bioinformatics widget collection. It ships inside Dash apps, but every widget is **also** a standalone *figure generator*: each call returns a regular `plotly.graph_objects.Figure`, which renders inline in Quarto / Jupyter exactly like any other Plotly chart. Hover for SNP IDs, scroll-zoom into peaks, no server required.

```bash
pip install dash-bio
```

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-7"}
# the canonical alias in the docs and tutorials
import dash_bio as dashbio

# we'll reuse loaders from the deck setup chunk:
#   load_gwas("height")     -> Manhattan widget
#   load_deseq2("drought")  -> Volcano widget
#   load_expression()       -> Clustergram widget
```

Reach for `dash-bio` when you want **interactivity** (hover tooltips, zoom, pan) and you'd rather assemble the chart in one line than rebuild the day-2 matplotlib version. For static, paper-ready figures the day-2 matplotlib sections still win on control.


<!-- slide 34 -->
## The Catalogue {.smaller}

[DashBio · catalogue]{.eyebrow}

### Six widgets we'll touch — each one parallels a day-1 or day-2 chart

::: {.keybox}
[The widgets]{.tl}

- **`ManhattanPlot`** — interactive Manhattan with hover-for-SNP. Parallels day-2 `_04_manhattan.qmd`.
- **`VolcanoPlot`** — interactive volcano with effect-size + significance cutoffs. Parallels day-1 `_07_volcano.qmd`.
- **`Clustergram`** — heatmap + row/column dendrograms (Plotly's `sns.clustermap`). Parallels day-3 `_01_pycomplexheatmap.qmd`.
- **`Circos`** — link diagram on a circular ideogram. Parallels day-2 `_06_pycirclize.qmd`.
- **`AlignmentChart`** — multiple-sequence alignment viewer. Parallels day-3 `_04_pymsaviz.qmd`.
- **`NeedlePlot`** — lollipops for variant effects along a protein. Parallels day-1 lollipop variants.
:::

The pattern is the same for every widget: hand it a dataframe (or string), name the columns / kwargs, and the call returns a Plotly `Figure`. Whatever you can do with a Plotly figure — `update_layout`, `update_traces`, `to_html` — works on the DashBio output.


<!-- slide 35 -->
## ManhattanPlot · One-Line Build {.smaller}

[DashBio · Manhattan]{.eyebrow}

### Hand it the GWAS table, name the four columns, done

DashBio's `ManhattanPlot` takes the same GWAS table we built up by hand in day-2 (`chrom`, `pos`, `pval`, `snp`). The horizontal threshold lines and the two-tone chromosome colours are drawn **for you**; hover tooltips expose every SNP's rsID.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-5|7-13"}
import dash_bio as dashbio                          # the package alias
import numpy as np                                  # for -log10 threshold

gwas = load_gwas("height")                          # chrom, pos, pval, snp
gwas.head(3)                                        # quick peek at the columns

# CALL the widget — every kwarg names a column
fig = dashbio.ManhattanPlot(
    dataframe=gwas,                                 # tidy GWAS table
    chrm="chrom",                                   # chromosome column
    bp="pos",                                       # base-pair position
    p="pval",                                       # raw p-value
    snp="snp",                                      # hover label per dot
    gene=None)                                      # no gene column in our table
fig                                                 # render inline (no .show())
```

`ManhattanPlot` handles the cumulative position offset, the two-tone parity colouring, and the genome-wide / suggestive threshold lines on its own — all four steps from the day-2 build, collapsed into one call.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
import dash_bio as dashbio                          # widget library

gwas = load_gwas("height")                          # tidy GWAS frame
fig = dashbio.ManhattanPlot(                        # CALL: one-line widget
    dataframe=gwas,
    chrm="chrom", bp="pos", p="pval", snp="snp", gene=None)
fig.update_layout(                                  # match the deck theme
    paper_bgcolor=CREAM, plot_bgcolor=CREAM,
    font=dict(family="IBM Plex Mono", color=INK, size=11),
    height=420, margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=30, b=10))
fig
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 36 -->
## ManhattanPlot · Style on Palette {.smaller}

[DashBio · Manhattan polish]{.eyebrow}

### Move the thresholds, recolour the hits, match the Economist look

The widget exposes a small but useful set of style kwargs: `genomewideline_value` and `suggestiveline_value` to relocate the dashed thresholds; `highlight_color` to recolour the dots that cross the genome-wide line. We point both colour args at the deck palette so the figure lives in the same world as the day-2 matplotlib version.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-13|15-18"}
import dash_bio as dashbio                          # widget library
import numpy as np                                  # for -log10()
gwas = load_gwas("height")                          # same GWAS table

# CALL the widget with explicit style args
fig = dashbio.ManhattanPlot(
    dataframe=gwas,
    chrm="chrom", bp="pos", p="pval", snp="snp", gene=None,
    genomewideline_value=-np.log10(5e-8),           # canonical Bonferroni line
    suggestiveline_value=-np.log10(1e-5),           # softer 1e-5 cutoff
    highlight_color=RED,                            # the spotlight on hits
    point_size=6,                                   # smaller dots, less crowding
    title="Height GWAS — interactive")              # editorial headline

# match the deck theme (cream paper, plex mono)
fig.update_layout(
    paper_bgcolor=CREAM, plot_bgcolor=CREAM,
    font=dict(family="IBM Plex Mono", color=INK, size=11))
```

Compared with the day-2 hand-built version: same picture, ~5 lines instead of ~25, plus hover-for-rsID out of the box. The trade-off is control — you can't easily re-style individual dots the way matplotlib lets you.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
import dash_bio as dashbio                          # widget library
gwas = load_gwas("height")                          # GWAS table
fig = dashbio.ManhattanPlot(                        # CALL with styling
    dataframe=gwas,
    chrm="chrom", bp="pos", p="pval", snp="snp", gene=None,
    genomewideline_value=-np.log10(5e-8),
    suggestiveline_value=-np.log10(1e-5),
    highlight_color=RED,
    point_size=6,
    title="Height GWAS — interactive")
fig.update_layout(
    paper_bgcolor=CREAM, plot_bgcolor=CREAM,
    font=dict(family="IBM Plex Mono", color=INK, size=11),
    height=420, margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=40, b=10))
fig
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 37 -->
## VolcanoPlot · One-Line Build {.smaller}

[DashBio · Volcano]{.eyebrow}

### log2FoldChange vs −log10(p), with the four-quadrant story drawn for you

`VolcanoPlot` is the same pattern: hand it the DESeq2 table, name the columns, and the dashed effect-size + significance lines are drawn for you. Hover shows the gene name on every dot.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-6|8-15"}
import dash_bio as dashbio                          # widget library
import numpy as np                                  # for -log10 threshold
de = load_deseq2("drought")                         # gene, log2FoldChange, pvalue, padj

# quick peek at the columns the widget needs
de[["gene", "log2FoldChange", "pvalue"]].head(3)

# CALL the widget — every kwarg names a column or threshold
fig = dashbio.VolcanoPlot(
    dataframe=de,                                   # the DE results
    effect_size="log2FoldChange",                   # x-axis column
    p="pvalue",                                     # y-axis column (raw p)
    snp="gene",                                     # hover label per dot
    gene=None,                                      # no separate gene column
    effect_size_line=[-1, 1],                       # |log2FC| > 1 cutoff
    genomewideline_value=-np.log10(0.05))           # p < 0.05 line
fig                                                 # render inline
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
import dash_bio as dashbio                          # widget library
de = load_deseq2("drought")                         # DE results
fig = dashbio.VolcanoPlot(                          # CALL
    dataframe=de,
    effect_size="log2FoldChange",
    p="pvalue",
    snp="gene",
    gene=None,
    effect_size_line=[-1, 1],
    genomewideline_value=-np.log10(0.05))
fig.update_layout(                                  # match deck theme
    paper_bgcolor=CREAM, plot_bgcolor=CREAM,
    font=dict(family="IBM Plex Mono", color=INK, size=11),
    height=420, margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=30, b=10))
fig
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 38 -->
## Clustergram · Heatmap + Dendrograms {.smaller}

[DashBio · Clustergram]{.eyebrow}

### A 20 × 12 slice of the expression matrix so the labels are readable

`Clustergram` is Plotly's interactive `sns.clustermap`. It runs hierarchical clustering on both axes, draws dendrograms top + left, and exposes `color_threshold` to cut clades into coloured branches. We slice the matrix down to **20 genes × 12 samples** so the labels stay legible on a deck slide.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-6|8-16"}
import dash_bio as dashbio                          # widget library
expr = load_expression()                            # 40 × 24 log2 TPM

# take the most variable 20 genes and the first 12 samples to keep it readable
top20 = expr.var(axis=1).nlargest(20).index         # most variable genes
m = expr.loc[top20, expr.columns[:12]]              # 20 × 12 slice

# CALL the widget — column_labels / row_labels feed the axis ticks
fig = dashbio.Clustergram(
    data=m.values,                                  # numpy matrix
    column_labels=list(m.columns),                  # sample IDs (top)
    row_labels=list(m.index),                       # gene names (right)
    color_threshold={"row": 1.2, "col": 1.2},       # where to cut dendrograms
    height=460, width=620,                          # widget dimensions
    color_map=[[0.0, BLUE], [0.5, CREAM],           # diverging blue↔cream↔red
               [1.0, RED]])
fig                                                 # render inline
```

`color_threshold` is the one knob that pays for itself: pick a height in the dendrogram and every branch below it gets its own colour, so coordinated clusters jump out.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
import dash_bio as dashbio                          # widget library

expr = load_expression()                            # 40 × 24 log2 TPM
top20 = expr.var(axis=1).nlargest(20).index         # most variable genes
m = expr.loc[top20, expr.columns[:12]]              # 20 × 12 slice

fig = dashbio.Clustergram(                          # CALL
    data=m.values,
    column_labels=list(m.columns),
    row_labels=list(m.index),
    color_threshold={"row": 1.2, "col": 1.2},
    height=460, width=620,
    color_map=[[0.0, BLUE], [0.5, CREAM], [1.0, RED]])
fig.update_layout(                                  # match deck theme
    paper_bgcolor=CREAM, plot_bgcolor=CREAM,
    font=dict(family="IBM Plex Mono", color=INK, size=9),
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=10, b=10))
fig
```
:::
::::

## AlignmentChart · A Brief Aside {.smaller}

[DashBio · AlignmentChart]{.eyebrow}

### MSA viewer that eats Clustal / FASTA strings

`AlignmentChart` reads a **string** in Clustal or FASTA format and renders the alignment with per-residue colouring, a consensus row, and a coverage track. Hover any column for the per-position counts. It's the lightweight cousin of pyMSAviz — full coverage of MSAs is in `_04_pymsaviz.qmd`.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-10|12-17"}
import dash_bio as dashbio                          # widget library

# a tiny synthetic MSA in FASTA format (5 sequences × 30 columns)
fasta = (
    ">seq1\nMKTIIALSYIFCLVFADYKDDDDK--AAGGT\n"
    ">seq2\nMKTIIALSYIFCLVFADYKDDDDK--AAGGT\n"
    ">seq3\nMKTILALSYIFCLVFADYKDDDDK--AAGGT\n"
    ">seq4\nMKTIIALSYAFCLVFADYKDDDDK--ARGGT\n"
    ">seq5\nMKTIVALSYIFCLVFADYKDDDDK--AAGGT\n")

# CALL the widget — `data=` is the alignment string itself
fig = dashbio.AlignmentChart(
    data=fasta,                                     # FASTA string
    height=320,                                     # widget pixel height
    showconsensus=True,                             # consensus row underneath
    showconservation=True)                          # per-column conservation bar
fig                                                 # render inline
```

For a single quick look at a small alignment, this is the cheapest possible viewer. For publication MSAs with custom colour schemes and feature overlays, pyMSAviz is the better choice (see day-3 `_04`).
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
import dash_bio as dashbio                          # widget library
fasta = (                                           # tiny synthetic MSA
    ">seq1\nMKTIIALSYIFCLVFADYKDDDDK--AAGGT\n"
    ">seq2\nMKTIIALSYIFCLVFADYKDDDDK--AAGGT\n"
    ">seq3\nMKTILALSYIFCLVFADYKDDDDK--AAGGT\n"
    ">seq4\nMKTIIALSYAFCLVFADYKDDDDK--ARGGT\n"
    ">seq5\nMKTIVALSYIFCLVFADYKDDDDK--AAGGT\n")
fig = dashbio.AlignmentChart(                       # CALL
    data=fasta,
    height=320,
    showconsensus=True,
    showconservation=True)
fig
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 40 -->
## DashBio · Takeaway {.smaller}

[DashBio · recap]{.eyebrow}

### Plotly figures, one line each

::: {.takeaway}
[The recipe]{.tl}
1. **`import dash_bio as dashbio`** — every widget lives behind one alias.
2. **Hand it a dataframe** and name the columns (`chrm`, `bp`, `p`, `snp` for Manhattan; `effect_size`, `p`, `snp` for Volcano; raw `data` array for Clustergram).
3. **The return value is a Plotly `Figure`** — `update_layout`, `update_traces`, hover, zoom all work out of the box.

**Compare with day-2:** reach for `dash-bio` when you want **interactivity** (hover tooltips, scroll-zoom) and you're happy with the default Plotly look. For **publication-grade static** figures with bespoke colouring and labels, the day-2 matplotlib builds (`_04_manhattan`, `_07_volcano` from day-1) still win on control.
:::
